headline: Chikayoru is 近い (chikai, “close”) plus 寄る (yoru, “to approach, get closer”).
Kizuku is, by surface analysis, 杵 (ki, “mallet, pounder, pestle”) plus 築く (tsuku, “to build up”): “to make something using a pounder or mallet”.
Kage is an unbound apophonic form, from Proto-Japonic *kankay, cognate with 陰 (kage, “shadow”).
Hai, “lung”, is from Middle Chinese 肺.
Tekisetsu is 適 (teki, “suitable, fit, proper”) plus 切 (setsu, “in close contact”).
Hankei, a radius, is 半 (han, “half”) plus 径 (kei, “diameter”).
Yubiwa is 指 (yubi, “finger”) plus 輪 (wa, “ring”).
Sakki is a shift from 先 (saki).
Ojigi is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 辞儀 (jigi, “bow”).
Kotowaza is 言 (koto) plus 業 (waza).
Hatake is first attested in the Man'yōshū, completed sometime after 759 CE; compare Korean 밭 (bat, “dry field”).
Aisukurīmu is simply English “ice cream”.
Koshō is from Chinese 胡椒 (hújiāo).
Donburi has two possible origins: 慳貪振り鉢 (kendon-buri-bachi, “greedy” bowl) with the ken elided, or the onomatopoeia どんぶり for something heavy plunking into deep water.
Taishō is 対 (tai, “place in opposition and compare”) plus 照 (shō, “check one thing against another”).
Kakaku is a Middle Chinese compound, 價格 (MC kaeH kaek).
Jettoki is ジェット (jetto, “jet”) plus 機 (-ki, “machine, (especially) aircraft”).
Mitomeru is thought to be 見 (mi, “seeing”) plus 留める (tomeru, “to hold, to keep”): “to keep one's vision on”.
Are is あ (a, “that, yon”) plus れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives), from older kare.
Moderu is called an internationalism; see English model.
Bōenkyō is 望遠 (bōen, “long-distance viewing”) plus 鏡 (-kyō, “lens”).
Fukameru is the root of 深い (fukai, “deep, profound”) plus -meru, from Classical Japanese 深む (fukamu).
Tasukaru is the mediopassive or spontaneous counterpart to 助ける (tasukeru).
Gaka is 画 (ga, “picture, drawing, painting”) plus 家 (-ka, “expert, professional, performer”), first cited to 1799.
Sei, “true”, is from Middle Chinese 正, the kan'on reading, so likely not as old as the shō reading.
Josei was repurposed from nyoshō in the Meiji period (1868–1912), using the newer kan'on readings.
Yubi is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonpE.
Heiwa is a rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), first attested in the Meiji era.
Mimau is 見 (mi) plus 舞う (mau).
Bussō is a pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物騒がしい (monosawagashii).
Kuwaeru is from Classical Japanese 咥ふ (kufafu), possibly related to 食う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”).
